title: From soil to Om
hook: the Chandogya follows a chain from the ground under your feet up to the chant, and finds Om at the end
carry: om is the essence of all essences

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sama Veda: verses from the Rig Veda set to melody, opening with come, Agni, to the feast.

Orange juice in a carton. Before that, oranges in a crate. Before that, a tree; before that, rain and soil. Every glass at breakfast sits at the end of a chain nobody follows back. One old text follows a chain like that, link by link, from the ground up, but it isn't tracing breakfast. It's tracing a song. The Chandogya Upanishad belongs to the Sama Veda, and right at its start it asks what the very best part of everything is, and keeps going until it reaches the chant itself.
screen: `A GLASS OF JUICE, A CHAIN BEHIND IT.` → `ONE TEXT TRACES A SONG.` → `THE CHAIN THAT ENDS IN A CHANT.`

segments.voice: The Chandogya opens with the udgitha, the high chant, the part of a Sama Veda song the lead singer sends up. It says, in paraphrase: let a person meditate on the syllable Om as the udgitha, for the chant begins with Om. Then comes the chain. The essence of all beings is the earth. The essence of the earth is water. Of water, plants. Of plants, the human being. Of the human being, speech. Of speech, the Rig Veda's verses. Of the Rig Veda, the saman, the melody. And of the saman, the udgitha, which is Om. Each link is the rasa, the juice, the essence, of the one before. And the text crowns the last one: this, it says, is the essence of all essences, the highest. That's the teaching. For Hindus, Om isn't a warm-up noise in front of a prayer. It's the heart of all sacred sound. That's why Vedic recitation traditionally begins with Om, and why so many prayers and mantras in Hindu homes still open with it. And notice where the chain starts: with dirt. The Upanishad doesn't float the sacred syllable above ordinary things; it grows it from soil, water and food, through a body and a voice. So when a grandmother says Om before her prayer, many teachers would say she's starting at the heart of the whole chain, field and all.
screen: `THE UDGITHA: THE HIGH CHANT.` · `EARTH, WATER, PLANTS, PEOPLE, SPEECH.` · `VERSE, THEN MELODY, THEN OM.` · then, large: `OM: THE ESSENCE OF ALL ESSENCES.`

segments.voice: Sit tall. Feel the ground under you, then the water in you, then the last thing you ate, grown somewhere, then yourself here, walking the chain link by link. Then, as many Hindus do before a prayer, say Om slowly on the out-breath, three times if you like, letting it rise from the chest; if Om isn't yours, a quiet hum will do. Rest in the quiet after each one. If you pray, let your prayer begin from there.
The Sama Veda as song. In the Chandogya, the melody is the essence of the verse, and Om, the heart of the chant, is the essence of all essences. Today's word.
screen: `THE SAMA VEDA AS SONG — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: om is the essence of all essences. The chain starts in the soil. Back tomorrow, same hill.

notes: Paraphrase of Chandogya 1.1.1–2: confirm the order of the chain (beings → earth → water → plants → person → speech → ṛc → sāman → udgītha) and the gloss of rasa as 'essence'.
Udgītha described as 'the part of a Sama Veda song the lead singer sends up' is a simplification of the udgātṛ's portion of the chant; confirm.
Max Müller's 1879 Upanishads translation is public domain but is not on the validator's list, so all English is paraphrase.
'Every Om, in this reading, has a field behind it' is an interpretive line; cut if a Keeper finds it too loose.
